label: Reflection Similarity Shape Spaces
notes: This chapter, printed pages 110 through 129, builds the reflection shape space by quotienting landmark configurations by the full orthogonal group together with translation and scale. We treat a shape and its mirror image as identical, the natural choice when handedness carries no biological or physical meaning.

label: When a Mirror Image Is the Same Shape
notes: Many objects come with no canonical handedness, so a left configuration and its reflection should count as one shape. Including reflections in the quotient group removes the orientation label, collapsing the two enantiomorphs onto a single point of the reflection shape space and simplifying inference.

label: From Configuration to Quotient
notes: We start with k labelled landmarks in m dimensions, center to kill translation, and scale to unit size. The remaining nuisance is the orthogonal group acting on the right. Quotienting by the full orthogonal group rather than only the rotations yields the reflection shape space directly.

label: The Orthogonal Group Quotient
notes: The reflection shape space is the orbit space of preshapes under the full orthogonal group. Because that group contains reflections, orbits are larger than in the Kendall rotation case, and the resulting quotient embeds cleanly for any ambient dimension m, not only the planar case.

label: The Gram Matrix Is O(m)-Invariant
notes: Replacing the centered scaled configuration by its Gram matrix of landmark inner products erases the orthogonal action entirely, since an orthogonal factor cancels against its transpose. The Gram matrix is therefore a complete invariant coordinate for the reflection shape, capturing every distance and angle among the landmarks.

label: Embedding into the PSD Cone
notes: The Gram map sends each reflection shape to a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix of rank at most m. This is an equivariant embedding into a Euclidean matrix space, so extrinsic statistics on the curved shape space reduce to ordinary linear algebra on symmetric matrices followed by a projection back.

label: Extrinsic Mean via Top Eigenstructure
notes: The extrinsic mean is obtained by averaging the embedded Gram matrices in the ambient symmetric space and projecting that Euclidean average onto the rank-m positive semidefinite set. The projection keeps the leading m eigenvalues and eigenvectors, so the population mean shape is read directly from the dominant spectrum.

label: Existence and Uniqueness
notes: The projection onto rank-m positive semidefinite matrices is single valued exactly when the m-th and the next eigenvalue of the average Gram matrix are distinct. Under this spectral gap the extrinsic mean exists and is unique, and the distribution is then called nonfocal, guaranteeing a well defined estimator.

label: Central Limit Theorem
notes: The sample extrinsic mean is the projection of the sample average Gram matrix. A delta method through the smooth projection map turns the ordinary multivariate central limit theorem in matrix space into asymptotic normality on the tangent space of the embedded reflection shape space, with an estimable covariance.

label: Two-Sample Tests
notes: To compare two populations we embed both, form their sample extrinsic means, and study the difference of projected Gram matrices in the tangent chart. The asymptotic normality from the central limit theorem yields a chi-squared Wald statistic, giving a nonparametric two-sample test for equality of reflection mean shapes.

label: Matched Pairs and Diagnostics
notes: For matched pairs we embed each member, take within-pair differences in the tangent chart, and test whether their mean vanishes. A residual that returns to the rank-m cone certifies the projection stayed on the manifold, the diagnostic the notebook uses to confirm the geometry was respected.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Reflection shape spaces identify mirror images, embed through the orthogonal-invariant Gram matrix into the positive semidefinite cone, and support extrinsic means, central limit theorems, and tests via the top-m spectrum. The construction works for every dimension m, setting up the projective shape spaces of the next chapter.
